planting.note: Set rooted softwood cuttings or nursery plants into well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in a cool, rocky site that mimics its high-elevation Appalachian heath-bald habitat.

directions: Plant in acidic, well-drained soil amended with pine bark or leaf mold, mulching to keep roots cool and moist. This low, colony-forming shrub is distinguished from other blueberries by the fine hairs covering its young twigs and leaf undersides, a trait that helps it withstand the exposed, rocky summits where it naturally grows. It spreads slowly by underground rhizomes rather than producing a single central crown, so give it room to form a patch over time. The small, dark berries are edible but sparse, making this species more valuable as a rare native conservation planting than a heavy fruit producer.

planting.note: Plant in sheltered, humus-rich, lime-free soil with reliable moisture, since this Himalayan species resents both drought and hard freezes.

directions: This dwarf, mat-forming shrub from the eastern Himalaya hugs the ground on wiry, bristly stems clothed in tiny rounded leaves, making it a favorite of rock-garden and ericaceous-bed collectors rather than a fruit crop. Grow it in cool, consistently moist, acidic soil in light woodland shade, protecting it from drying winds and the harshest winter cold. Small pink-tinged bell flowers appear in late spring followed by sparse purple-black berries that are edible but incidental to its ornamental, carpet-forming habit. Top-dress annually with leaf mold to maintain the cool, humid root conditions it needs.

planting.note: Install bare-root or container plants in fall so roots establish over the rainy season before the dry chaparral summer sets in.

directions: A spiny, deciduous shrub of California oak woodland and chaparral, this gooseberry bears small pendant pink-to-white flowers in late winter that are an early nectar source for hummingbirds and native bees. Once established, it needs little to no irrigation, thriving on winter rain alone and going summer-dormant in the driest months. Plant it where its arching, prickly branches have room to form a loose thicket, ideally in dappled shade under oaks on the coast or in a bit more sun inland. The small, spiny-coated berries are edible once fully ripe but are of more value to wildlife and native landscaping than as a cultivated fruit crop.

planting.note: Plant into lean, well-drained soil in an open site, since this high-desert native resents heavy, wet clay more than it resents cold.

directions: Named for the clusters of pure white, bell-shaped flowers it produces in early spring well before its leaves fully expand, this spiny shrub is native to sagebrush steppe and rocky foothills of the interior Pacific Northwest and Great Basin. It tolerates poor, rocky, alkaline-leaning soils and extreme temperature swings, making it useful for xeric native plantings and erosion-prone slopes. Space plants generously to allow for its arching, thorny canes, and avoid summer overhead watering once established. The dark purple berries that follow are tart and seedy, valued mainly by wildlife and native-plant foragers rather than as a dessert fruit.
sources: Flora of the Pacific Northwest (Hitchcock & Cronquist)

planting.note: Site in a sheltered woodland position with acidic, moisture-retentive soil, as this Yunnan native prefers mild, humid winters over hard freezes.

directions: A compact, slow-growing evergreen shrub from the mountains of Yunnan, China, this species is grown chiefly for its tidy habit, small glossy box-like leaves, and clusters of pale pink urn-shaped flowers rather than for its fruit. It is closely related to the better-known Vaccinium moupinense but stays denser and more rounded, making it suitable for sheltered rock gardens and ericaceous borders. Give it acidic, well-drained but moisture-retentive soil and protection from drying winds and the coldest winter extremes. The small dark berries that follow flowering are edible but sparse, so treat this primarily as a specialty ornamental foliage shrub.
